data: The course is designed for a college level audience, and is intended as a comprehensive foundation for advanced courses that students may opt for in the future. Course topics will be contemporary, and will focus on conceptual understanding and not encyclopedic detail. The course will involve the study of microbes of the various taxa, viz viruses, protozoans, bacteria, algae, and fungi, their place in the evolutionary order of things, their diversity and distribution, and their relevance in the Anthropocene. The course will use a bacterial-centric approach in its treatment of microbial taxonomy, metabolism, genetics, multiplication, and growth. Industrial, agricultural, environmental, and clinical applications and value will be highlighted wherever relevant using microbial archetypes; this will include certain clinically important pathogens and their control, fermentation as an industrial process, the use of engineered microbes in waste processing and pollution control, and agricultural pests and pest controls. The contribution of microbes to human health (as the microbiome, and as probiotics), and societal and environmental health (as degraders of waste) will be discussed. Students will be taught to isolate bacteria from their surroundings, and to examine, identify, propagate, and preserve them. Emphasis will be placed on bacterial genetics, especially the bacterial extra-chromosomal DNA (the plasmid) and its centricity in recombinant DNA techniques or genetic engineering. The course will enable the student to understand the multitudes of microbes cohabiting with humans, and the nature and degree of interaction between the two. Care will be taken to cross-reference concepts taught in this course with relevant concepts taught in earlier courses.
